claim: The southern house mosquito, Culex quinquefasciatus, utilizes two odorant receptors, CquiOR10 and CquiOR2, narrowly tuned to oviposition attractants and well conserved among mosquito species.
source: The southern house mosquito, Culex quinquefasciatus, utilizes two odorant receptors, CquiOR10 and CquiOR2, narrowly tuned to oviposition attractants and well conserved among mosquito species.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing the specificity of these receptors and references to their conservation across species.

claim: CquiOR10 detects skatole and CquiOR2 detects indole with reciprocal specificity.
source: They detect skatole and indole, respectively, with reciprocal specificity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response curves in Figure 1 showing CquiOR10 responds preferentially to skatole and CquiOR2 to indole.

claim: TM2 was identified as a specificity determinant through transmembrane domain swapping experiments.
source: We swapped the transmembrane (TM) domains of CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 and identified TM2 as a specificity determinant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chimeric receptor testing showing that swapping TM2 altered receptor specificity.

claim: CquiOR10A73L behaves like CquiOR2 in terms of ligand specificity.
source: With additional mutations, we showed that CquiOR10A73L behaved like CquiOR2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3I showing CquiOR10A73L responds preferentially to indole like CquiOR2.

claim: CquiOR2L74A recapitulates CquiOR10 specificity.
source: Conversely, CquiOR2L74A recapitulated CquiOR10 specificity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3J showing CquiOR2L74A responds preferentially to skatole like CquiOR10.

claim: Structural models of CquiOR10 and CquiOR10A73L were generated using RoseTTAFold and AlphaFold.
source: Next, we generated structural models of CquiOR10 and CquiOR10A73L using RoseTTAFold and AlphaFold and docked skatole and indole using RosettaLigand.
evidence: The models are shown in Figure 6 and were generated using computational prediction methods.

claim: Modeling studies suggest space-filling constraints around A73 in CquiOR10.
source: These modeling studies suggested space-filling constraints around A73.
evidence: This hypothesis is based on computational docking studies and structural analysis shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: CquiOR10 mutants with bulkier residues (Ile, Val) at position 73 are insensitive to skatole and indole.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, CquiOR10 mutants with a bulkier residue (Ile, Val) were insensitive to skatole and indole
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of response in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B, with functional expression confirmed by OLC12 responses.

claim: CquiOR10A73G retains specificity to skatole and shows a more robust response than wildtype CquiOR10.
source: whereas CquiOR10A73G retained the specificity to skatole and showed a more robust response than the wildtype receptor CquiOR10.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Leu to Gly mutation of CquiOR2 (CquiOR2L74G) reverts the specificity to skatole.
source: On the other hand, Leu to Gly mutation of the indole receptor CquiOR2 reverted the specificity to skatole.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F showing preferential response to skatole.

claim: CquiOR10A73L, CquiOR2, and CquiOR2L74I are insensitive to 3-ethylindole.
source: Lastly, CquiOR10A73L, CquiOR2, and CquiOR2L74I were insensitive to 3-ethylindole
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of response to 3-ethylindole shown in Figure 9.

claim: CquiOR2L74A and CquiOR2L74G gained activity to 3-ethylindole.
source: whereas CquiOR2L74A and CquiOR2L74G gained activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-dependent responses to 3-ethylindole shown in Figure 9.

claim: CquiOR10A73G gives more robust responses to 3-ethylindole than CquiOR10.
source: Additionally, CquiOR10A73G gave more robust responses to 3-ethylindole than CquiOR10.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative response data in Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The specificity of CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 is mediated by a single amino acid substitution.
source: Thus, we suggest the specificity of these receptors is mediated by a single amino acid substitution, leading to finely tuned volumetric space to accommodate specific oviposition attractants.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mutagenesis experiments showing that single point mutations at position 73/74 reverse receptor specificity.

claim: Insect odorant receptors have inverse topology compared to G-protein-coupled receptors, with a cytosolic N-terminus and an extracellular C-terminus.
source: Unlike mammalian olfactory receptors, insect ORs and Orco have inverse topologies compared to G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), with a cytosolic N-terminus and an extracellular C-terminus (Benton et al., 2006; Lundin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on insect OR topology.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of Orco homomer from Apocrypta bakeri (AbakOrco) was determined.
source: One of the major breakthroughs in the fields of insect olfaction in the last two decades since the discovery of ORs (Leal, 2020) was the determination of the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the Orco homomer from the parasitic fig wasp, Apocrypta bakeri, AbakOrco (Butterwick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Butterwick et al., 2018 publication.

claim: The structure of MhraOR5 from Machilis hrabei was solved.
source: Subsequently, the structure for a promiscuous OR from the evolutionarily primitive (Apterygota, wingless) jumping bristletail, Machilis hrabei, MhraOR5, was solved (DelMarmol et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the DelMarmol et al., 2021 publication.

claim: Culex quinquefasciatus transmits pathogens causing filariasis and various encephalitis.
source: The southern house mosquito, Culex quinquefasciatus, transmits pathogens causing filariasis and various encephalitis (Nasci and Miller, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on mosquito-borne diseases.

claim: Culex quinquefasciatus is a significant bridge vector for West Nile virus in urbanized centers in the Western United States.
source: Due to its opportunistic feeding on avian and mammalian hosts, Cx. quinquefasciatus is a significant bridge vector in urbanized centers in the Western United States, particularly southern California (Andreadis, 2012; Syed and Leal, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on West Nile virus transmission.

claim: The genome of Culex quinquefasciatus has the most extensive repertoire of OR genes among mosquito species.
source: The genome of the southern house mosquito, Cx. quinquefasciatus (Arensburger et al., 2010), has the most extensive repertoire of OR genes (Leal et al., 2013) among mosquito species.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies comparing OR gene numbers across mosquito species.

claim: Culex quinquefasciatus has 180 OR genes.
source: The genomes of Anopheles darlingi, the malaria mosquito, Anopheles gambiae, the yellow fever mosquito, Aedes aegypti, the Asian tiger mosquito, Aedes albopictus, and the southern house mosquito contain 18 (Marinotti et al., 2013), 79 (Hill et al., 2002), 117–131 (Bohbot et al., 2007; Nene et al., 2007), 158 (Chen et al., 2015), and 180 (Arensburger et al., 2010) OR genes, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Arensburger et al., 2010 genomic study.

claim: 177 OR transcripts were found in Culex quinquefasciatus.
source: Of those, 61 transcripts were found in An. gambiae (Pitts et al., 2011), 107 in Ae. aegypti (Matthews et al., 2018), and 177 in Cx. quinquefasciatus (Leal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Leal et al., 2013 transcriptomic study.

claim: Skatole and indole have been identified as oviposition attractants for Culex quinquefasciatus.
source: Skatole and indole are fecal products that have been identified as oviposition attractants for the southern house mosquito (Blackwell et al., 1993; Mboera et al., 2000; Millar et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies on mosquito oviposition.

claim: Skatole is a potent oviposition attractant in minute doses, whereas indole is active only at high doses.
source: Skatole is a potent oviposition attractant in minute doses, whereas indole is active only at high doses (Millar et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to behavioral studies on oviposition attractants.

claim: In all mosquito species and the housefly, OR10s are narrowly tuned to skatole and respond with lower sensitivity to indole.
source: Remarkably, in all mosquito species and the housefly, OR10s are narrowly tuned to skatole and respond with lower sensitivity to indole
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies of OR10 orthologs across species.

claim: Indole is the most potent ligand for OR2s, which give lower responses to skatole.
source: whereas indole is the most potent ligand for OR2s, which give lower responses to skatole.
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies of OR2 orthologs across species.

claim: CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 proteins share 49.5% amino acid identity.
source: CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 proteins have 377 and 375 amino acid residues, respectively, and share only 49.5% amino acid identity
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 61.9% of the amino acids in the predicted transmembrane domains of CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 are identical.
source: whereas 61.9% of the amino acids in the predicted transmembrane domains are identical (Supplementary file 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis of transmembrane domains.

claim: CquiOR10 is the second most sensitive Culex quinquefasciatus OR, second only to CquiOR36.
source: Given that CquiOR10 is the second most sensitive Cx. quinquefasciatus OR (second only to CquiOR36; Choo et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Choo et al., 2018 study comparing OR sensitivities.

claim: CquiOR10M2,7 emulates the response profile of the indole receptor CquiOR2.
source: Lastly, CquiOR10M2,7/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes responded to both skatole and indole with a reverse profile (Figure 3A). This dataset shows that CquiOR10M2,7 emulated the profile of the indole receptor CquiOR2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3A showing reversed specificity.

claim: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7 is more sensitive than CquiOR10M2,7 while maintaining selectivity to indole.
source: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes were indeed more sensitive while maintaining the selectivity to indole (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3B showing enhanced sensitivity to indole.

claim: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Outer retained the specificity of CquiOR10M2,5,6,7 with a more robust response to indole than skatole.
source: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Outer/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes retained the specificity of CquiOR10M2,5,6,7 with a more robust response to indole than skatole (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3C.

claim: Residues in the outer segment of TM2 are not specificity determinants.
source: These findings indicated that the residues in the outer segment of TM2 are not specificity determinants.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Outer retained indole specificity.

claim: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Mid;Inner restored the skatole-specific profile of CquiOR10.
source: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Mid;Inner restored the skatole-specific profile of CquiOR10 (Figure 3D), thus suggesting that amino acid residues in these segments are specificity determinants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3D showing restored skatole specificity.

claim: Amino acid residues in the middle and inner segments of TM2 are specificity determinants.
source: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Mid;Inner restored the skatole-specific profile of CquiOR10 (Figure 3D), thus suggesting that amino acid residues in these segments are specificity determinants.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that restoring these residues restored skatole specificity.

claim: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Inner reverted the specificity to skatole.
source: Oocytes co-expressing CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Inner and CquiOrco reverted the specificity to skatole (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3E showing skatole specificity.

claim: Residues in the predicted inner part of TM2 are critical for the chimeric receptor's specificity.
source: As a result, we concluded that residues in the predicted inner part of TM2 are critical for the chimeric receptor's specificity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that CquiOR10M2,5,6,7_Inner restored skatole specificity.

claim: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7T78I showed the same specificity as CquiOR10M2,5,6,7.
source: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7T78I/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes showed the same specificity as the chimeric receptor CquiOR10M2,5,6,7 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3F showing indole specificity.

claim: Rescuing the residue at position 78 did not affect CquiOR10M2,5,6,7 specificity.
source: Specifically, CquiOR10M2,5,6,7T78I gave a more robust response to indole than skatole, suggesting that rescuing the residue at 78 did not affect CquiOR10M2,5,6,7 specificity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that CquiOR10M2,5,6,7T78I retained indole specificity.

claim: CquiOR10M2,5,6,7L73A reverted the specificity to skatole.
source: By contrast, CquiOR10M2,5,6,7L73A/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes reverted the specificity to skatole (Figure 3G), thus behaving like the wildtype receptor CquiOR10 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3G showing skatole specificity.

claim: CquiOR10M7A73L shows a reverse, indole-specific profile.
source: The responses recorded from CquiOR10M7A73L/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes showed a reverse, indole-specific profile (Figure 3H), like the CquiOR2 profile (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3H showing indole specificity.

claim: Ala-73 is a single amino acid residue that determines CquiOR10 specificity.
source: Having identified a single amino acid residue in the chimeric receptor that switches the skatole/indole specificity, we tested the effect of single-point mutation on the specificity of the wildtype receptor CquiOR10
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mutagenesis experiments showing that A73L mutation reverses specificity.

claim: CquiOR10 has an EC50 of 3.6 µM for skatole and 29.9 µM for indole.
source: we tested the effect of single-point mutation on the specificity of the wildtype receptor CquiOR10 (EC50: skatole, 3.6 µM; indole 29.9 µM).
evidence: These EC50 values are derived from dose-response curve fitting of experimental data.

claim: CquiOR10A73L has an EC50 of 3.4 µM for indole and 53.7 µM for skatole.
source: CquiOR10A73L showed a reverse specificity, with dose-dependent responses to indole (Figure 3I) (EC50: indole, 3.4 µM; skatole 53.7 µM).
evidence: These EC50 values are derived from dose-response curve fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: CquiOR2 has an EC50 of 7.7 µM for indole and 16.4 µM for skatole.
source: Additionally, we obtained an equivalent single-point mutation in the indole-specific CquiOR2 (Figure 1B) (EC50: indole, 7.7 µM; skatole 16.4 µM).
evidence: These EC50 values are derived from dose-response curve fitting of experimental data.

claim: CquiOR2L74A has an EC50 of 8.5 µM for skatole and 27.6 µM for indole.
source: Thus, CquiOR2L74A/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes gave robust and specific responses to skatole (Figure 3J) (EC50: skatole, 8.5 µM; indole 27.6 µM).
evidence: These EC50 values are derived from dose-response curve fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: A single amino acid residue mediates reciprocal specificity in CquiOR10 and CquiOR2.
source: these findings demonstrate that these two mosquito odorant receptors, CquiOR10 and CquiOR2, have reciprocal specificity mediated by a single amino acid residue, Ala-73 and Leu-74, respectively.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive mutagenesis data showing that single point mutations reverse specificity in both receptors.

claim: CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 respond to phenol.
source: While CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 responded to phenol, 3,5-dimethylphenol activated only CquiOR10 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 3,5-dimethylphenol activates only CquiOR10 and not CquiOR2.
source: While CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 responded to phenol, 3,5-dimethylphenol activated only CquiOR10 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A single-point mutation in CquiOR10 (A73L) renders the receptor insensitive to 3,5-dimethylphenol.
source: A single-point mutation in CquiOR10 rendered the chimeric receptor insensitive to 3,5-dimethylphenol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CquiOR2L74A recapitulates the CquiOR10 response profile to 3,5-dimethylphenol.
source: By contrast, an equivalent mutation in CquiOR2 recapitulated the profile of CquiOR10 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CquiOR10 elicits stronger responses to 1-methylindole and 5-methylindole than to other methylindoles.
source: CquiOR10/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes elicited stronger responses when challenged with 1-methylindole and 5-methylindole than when stimulated with the other methylindoles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CquiOR2 elicits similarly lower responses when stimulated with methylindoles.
source: By contrast, CquiOR2/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes elicited similarly lower responses when stimulated with methylindoles (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CquiOR2L74A recapitulates the CquiOR10 response profile to methylindoles.
source: CquiOR2L74A with a single-point mutation to mimic OR10 receptor recapitulated CquiOR10 response profile (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A single amino acid residue determines a receptor's specificity toward ligands eliciting robust or small responses.
source: These data suggest that a single amino acid residue determines a receptor's specificity toward ligands eliciting robust or small responses.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the methylindole response data showing that the A73/L74 residue affects responses to multiple ligands.

claim: RoseTTAFold models of CquiOR10, CquiOR10A73L, CquiOR2, and CquiOR2A73L produced a transmembrane helix RMSD less than 1 Å.
source: RoseTTAFold models of CquiOR10, CquiOR10A73L, CquiOR2, and CquiOR2A73L produced a transmembrane helix root mean square deviation (RMSD) between α-Carbon atoms less than 1 Å across all 20 models (five models per odorant receptor)
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the computational models.

claim: CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 are structurally similar.
source: this suggests that the homologous CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 are structurally similar
evidence: This conclusion is based on the low RMSD values between the structural models.

claim: Single-point mutations should not cause great structural deviation from wildtype in CquiOR10 and CquiOR2.
source: and that single-point mutations should not cause great structural deviation from wildtype.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the low RMSD values between wildtype and mutant models.

claim: RoseTTAFold and AlphaFold models of CquiOR10 produced a transmembrane helix RMSD of 1.7 Å.
source: Comparing CquiOR10 models, RoseTTAFold and AlphaFold produced a transmembrane helix RMSD of 1.7 Å
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of models generated by the two methods.

claim: RosettaLigand can recapitulate the MhraOR5-eugenol structure with RMSD values ranging from 0.5 to 5.0 Å.
source: With this selection method, the RMSD of our MhraOR5-eugenol models relative to the experimental structure ranged from 0.5 to 5.0 Å (Supplementary file 1, Table 3).
evidence: This is based on docking validation studies using the experimentally determined MhraOR5 structure.

claim: The largest cluster of MhraOR5-eugenol models had an RMSD of 0.75 Å.
source: After using hdbscan cluster analysis (McInnes et al., 2017) to group structurally similar models, the largest cluster had a RMSD of 0.75 Å
evidence: This is based on cluster analysis of docking models.

claim: The lowest interface-energy MhraOR5-eugenol model had an RMSD of 2.4 Å.
source: while the lowest interface-energy model had a RMSD of 2.4 Å.
evidence: This is based on energy-based selection of docking models.

claim: RosettaLigand paired with hdbscan clustering can recapitulate the MhraOR5 structure and blindly select a near-native model.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that RosettaLigand paired with the hdbscan clustering method can recapitulate the MhraOR5 structure and blindly select a near-native model
evidence: This conclusion is based on the validation studies showing low RMSD values for docked models.

claim: Both indole and skatole can readily reorient themselves in a similar pore depth near residue 73.
source: Our modeling suggests that both indole and skatole can readily reorient themselves in a similar pore depth near residue 73, regardless of mutant or wildtype receptor.
evidence: This is based on analysis of docking models showing ligand positioning.

claim: Indole and skatole are positioned in the membrane-embedded pore, flanked by transmembrane helices S2, S4, S5, and S6.
source: Comparing the lowest interface-scoring model from each receptor–ligand complex, indole and skatole are positioned in the membrane-embedded pore, flanked by transmembrane helices S2, S4, S5, and S6
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural models shown in Figure 7.

claim: Indole and skatole show positional overlap in both CquiOR10-A73L and CquiOR10.
source: and show positional overlap in both and CquiOR10-A73L CquiOR10 (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural models shown in Figure 7 and supplements.

claim: Skatole and indole form contacts with CquiOR10 and CquiOr10A73L in a similar plane about a center of rotation.
source: In most models, skatole and indole form contacts with CquiOR10 and CquiOr10A73L in a similar plane about a center of rotation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of multiple docking models.

claim: The ligand-binding pocket is formed by TMs 2, 4, 5, and 6.
source: Protein–ligand interaction profiler (PLIP) analysis (Adasme et al., 2021) suggests that the bulk of favorable interactions are nonpolar, occasional hydrogen bonding with the odorant NH group, and occasional parallel pi stacking, with the ligand-binding pocket formed by TMs 2, 4, 5, and 6 (Figure 7—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is based on PLIP analysis of the docking models shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6.

claim: Skatole and indole do not form contacts with Ala-73 in CquiOR10 models.
source: We find of most importance skatole and indole not forming contacts with Ala-73 in CquiOR10 models (Supplementary file 1, Tables 6–14).
evidence: This is based on contact analysis of the docking models.

claim: In CquiOR17A73L models, skatole formed hydrophobic contacts with Leu-73 in 5 of 10 representative models.
source: By contrast, in the CquiOR17A73L models, skatole formed hydrophobic contacts with Leu-73 in 5 of the 10 representative models
evidence: This is based on contact analysis of the docking models.

claim: In CquiOR17A73L models, indole formed contacts with Leu-73 in 2 representative models.
source: while indole formed contacts with Leu-73 in 2 representative models (Supplementary file 1, Table 8).
evidence: This is based on contact analysis of the docking models.

claim: Ala-73 may indirectly affect specificity by modulating the volume of the binding pocket.
source: This suggests that Ala-73 may indirectly affect specificity by modulating the volume of the binding pocket (see Appendix 3).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that A73 does not directly contact ligands but affects specificity.

claim: There is approximately a 1 Å α-carbon outward shift of A73L in CquiOR10A73L compared to CquiOR10.
source: Structurally aligning CquiOR10 and CquiOR10A73L receptors by TM7b (Supplementary file 1, Table 15), demonstrates approximately a 1 Å α-carbon outward shift of A73L (Supplementary file 1, Table 16)
evidence: This is based on structural alignment analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: There is a tightly constrained space in CquiOR10 and an expanded space in CquiOR10A73L relative to the protein backbone.
source: suggesting a tightly constrained space in CquiOR10 and an expanded space in CquiOR10A73L relative to the protein backbone (Figure 8).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the structural analysis showing the outward shift of the residue.

claim: The difference in binding pocket volume between CquiOR10 and CquiOR10A73L is not ligand-induced, but rather independent of skatole or indole binding.
source: This difference in binding pocket volume is not ligand-induced, but rather independent of skatole or indole binding.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of apo structures showing the volume difference exists without ligands.

claim: CquiOR10A73I and CquiOR10A73V do not respond to skatole or indole.
source: Specifically, CquiOR10A73I/CquiOrco- and CquiOR10A73V/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes did not respond to skatole or indole (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of response shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mutations with bulkier residues (Ile, Val) at position 73 caused loss of binding to indole or skatole.
source: We concluded that mutations with these bulkier residues caused loss of binding to indole or skatole
evidence: This conclusion is based on the lack of response to ligands but retained response to OLC12.

claim: CquiOR10A73I and CquiOR10A73V receptors are functional as indicated by responses to OLC12.
source: given that these receptors were functional, as indicated by the potent responses elicited by the Orco ligand candidate OLC12, 2-{[4-Ethyl-5-(4-pyridinyl)–4 H-1,2,4-triazol-3-yl]sulfanyl}-N-(4-isopropylphenyl)acetamide (Chen and Luetje, 2012), also known as VUAA-3 (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the OLC12 responses shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: OR-Orco complexes are more sensitive to activation by Orco agonists than Orco homomers.
source: As previously demonstrated, OR-Orco complexes are more sensitive to activation by Orco agonists than are the Orco homomers (Chen and Luetje, 2012; Chen and Luetje, 2013; Choo et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2017; Chen and Luetje, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on OR-Orco complex pharmacology.

claim: CquiOR10A73G shows the same skatole specificity as the wildtype receptor.
source: On the other hand, CquiOR10A73G/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes showed the same skatole specificity as the wildtype receptor (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Skatole elicits stronger currents from CquiOR10A73G than from wildtype CquiOR10.
source: Interestingly, skatole elicited stronger currents recorded from CquiOR10A73G than the wildtype receptor CquiOR10 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative response data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: CquiOR10A73G has higher affinity for skatole when there is reduced constraint or increased volume of the binding pocket.
source: further implying a higher affinity for skatole when there is a reduced constraint, or increased volume, of the binding pocket.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that the Gly mutation increases response to skatole.

claim: CquiOR2 has 49.5% sequence identity and 71.7% sequence similarity to CquiOR10.
source: Since CquiOR2 is homologous to CquiOR10, we also propose that our space constraint structural hypothesis can be applied to CquiOR2. CquiOR2 has 49.5% sequence identity and 71.7% sequence similarity to CquiOR10.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: CquiOR2L74I retains the specificity of the wildtype receptor to indole.
source: Consistent with the relaxation of the space constraints, CquiOR2L74I retained the specificity of the wildtype receptor to indole
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CquiOR2L74G shows a reverse specificity profile with more robust response to skatole than indole.
source: whereas CquiOR2L74G showed a reverse specificity profile (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F), that is, more robust response to skatole than indole.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CquiOR2L74V generates nearly equal currents when stimulated with skatole and indole.
source: Interestingly, CquiOR2L74V/CquiOrco-expressing oocytes generated nearly equal, albeit small, currents when stimulated with the two oviposition attractants (skatole, 8.7 ± 2.7 nA; indole, 9.0 ± 2.5 nA at 100 µM; n = 3, p>0.9999, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test).
evidence: This is based on quantitative response measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: CquiOR10A73G elicits responses to 3-ethylindole higher than responses to indole.
source: A CquiOR10 mutant with a less space-filling residue, CquiOR10A73G, elicited responses to 3-ethylindole (526 ± 110 nA) higher than the responses to indole (205 ± 81 nA, at 100 µM)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: CquiOR10A73G responses to 3-ethylindole are less robust than skatole responses.
source: although less robust than the skatole responses (1939 ± 142 nA; all at 100 µM) (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: CquiOR2WT, CquiO10A73L, and CquiOR2L74I do not respond to 3-ethylindole.
source: By contrast, receptors with a bulkier residue (CquiOR2WT, CquiO10A73L, and CquiOR2L74I) did not respond to 3-ethylindole (Figure 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of response shown in Figure 9.

claim: CquiOR2L74A and CquiOR2L74G respond to 3-ethylindole in a dose-dependent manner.
source: However, CquiOR2 mutant with less space-filling residues, CquiOR2L74A and CquiOR2L74G, responded to 3-ethylindole in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 9.

claim: CquiOR10A73G elicits dose-dependent strong responses to 3-ethylindole compared to CquiOR10.
source: Additionally, CquiOR10A73G elicited dose-dependent strong responses to 3-ethylindole than CquiOR10 (Figure 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative dose-response data in Figure 9.

claim: A bulkier, non-natural ligand (3-ethylindole) elicits more robust responses when CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 residues at 73 and 74 are mutated to Gly.
source: In summary, the findings that a bulkier, non-natural ligand, elicited more robust responses when CquiOR10 and CquiOR2 residues at 73 and 74, respectively, were mutated into Gly are consistent with the space constraints hypothesis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the 3-ethylindole response data supporting the volumetric space hypothesis.

claim: The OCTOPUS prediction method accurately predicts transmembrane domains as validated by the AbakOrco structure.
source: The almost perfect overlap between OCTOPUS prediction and the AbakOrco structure (Figure 2B) validated not only our TM predictions (Figure 2A), but also the 21 chimeric ORs already tested when the structure of the coreceptor AbakOrco (Butterwick et al., 2018) was reported.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 14 chimeric receptors did not respond to skatole or indole.
source: Fourteen chimeric receptors did not respond to skatole or indole
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1, Table 2.

claim: 21 chimeric receptors retained the specificity to skatole.
source: and 21 receptors retained the specificity to skatole (Supplementary file 1, Table 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1, Table 2 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 36 chimeric receptors were tested in total.
source: We tested 36 chimeric receptors (see Supplementary file 1, Table 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1, Table 2.

claim: Insect ORs are the binding units in functional heteromeric cation channels formed with Orco.
source: The ORs are the binding units in functional heteromeric cation channels (Neuhaus et al., 2005) formed with an odorant receptor coreceptor (Orco) (Larsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on OR-Orco channel formation.

claim: Insect antennae are biosensors that allow detection of a plethora of compounds, some with extraordinary sensitivity and selectivity.
source: Their antennae are biosensors par excellence, allowing detection of a plethora of compounds, some with extraordinary sensitivity and selectivity (Kaissling, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on insect olfactory sensitivity.

claim: The insect olfactory system is comprised mainly of odorant-binding proteins, odorant-degrading enzymes, ionotropic receptors, and odorant receptors.
source: The insect olfactory system is comprised mainly of odorant-binding proteins, odorant-degrading enzymes, ionotropic receptors, and the ultimate gatekeepers of selectivity (Leal, 2013; Leal, 2016; Leal, 2020) – the odorant receptors (ORs) (Clyne et al., 1999; Gao and Chess, 1999; Vosshall et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews and original research on insect olfactory system components.
